nodes.name: Watercolor storybook cartoon
nodes.summary: Hand-painted 2D cartoon look: warm paper, soft bleeding watercolor washes, wobbly ink outlines, with clean saturated characters animated on top. The most completely documented style in the corpus.
nodes.detail:
The look is four stacked layers: a warm off-white paper ground (#FBF3E6), translucent washes with soft bleeding
edges, slightly wobbly ink outlines (#3A2A24 to #4A3428) on props but not on skies, and flat, saturated characters
drawn fresh every frame. Backgrounds stay light and warm or desaturated; the character is always the
highest-contrast thing on screen.

**Execute:** paint the set and props once with p5.brush on a hidden WEBGL canvas and cache them; composite moving
vector parts per frame on Canvas 2D; finish every frame with grain (overlay, about 0.26 to 0.28) and a warm
multiply vignette. Defaults: 1920x1080, 24 fps, 8 to 20 s, one set, a few props, about five beats per 15 s. Named
palettes exist for cozy room, meadow, night, forest and underwater. Lighting is only ever a `screen` tint on top.

**Why it works:** organic texture lives where it is cheap (static layers), crisp motion lives where the eye tracks.

**Failure modes:** paper halos around loosely clipped sprites, sawtooth bleed on long polygon edges, texture
boiling if layers are repainted per frame, muddy colour from source-over tints.

nodes.name: Never-cut morphing container film
nodes.summary: Product and UI motion in which one rounded container continuously morphs (pill, card, terminal, chart) while content swaps inside it, instead of cutting between separate graphics.
nodes.detail:
One object persists for the whole clip. Its width, height, corner radius and fill animate between states, and its
inner content swaps behind a brief blur. A cursor often motivates each change. The register appears as standalone
launch films ("product film UI motion") and as b-roll panels over talking heads.

**Execute:** write the state sequence as numeric targets; give each content layer its own enter and exit timing;
drive geometry with closed-form springs that have very small overshoot plus exponential easing; render with
subframe motion blur so fast morphs smear rather than strobe.

**Why it works:** continuity of form reads as designed motion and avoids the slide-deck look typical of AI output;
the eye never has to re-find the subject.

**Failure modes:** letters colliding while the container resizes, a weak opening frame, invented numbers in the
chart state (use relative bars and skeleton text until real data is supplied), default palette off-brand.

nodes.name: Beat-locked kinetic type showreel
nodes.summary: Short (around 15 s) launch films and showreels made of typography, shapes and UI moments that change on every musical beat, with a tight palette and a single typeface.
nodes.detail:
The dominant category in the prompt-motion gallery (kinetic type, shapes, particles, product UI, charts).

**Execute:** settle tempo and bars before anything else, for example 120 BPM, a change on every beat, the hook
inside bar one, the strongest moment in the last full bar and the end title in the final half bar. Use one
typeface (Geist or Inter, or one bold display face), at most three colours plus black and white, a warm off-white
or near-black ground and one consistent accent. Plan six to eight shots for 15 s. Animate per letter for word
morphs and give text separate in and out timing. Synthesize a track with a kick per beat and a riser into the
final bar.

**Why it works:** beat-matched change was the clearest observed difference between launch films and "feature
slideshows"; restraint in type and colour reads as premium.

**Failure modes:** one-line briefs give wildly variable results; unrequested glows, gradients, centred text and
particle bursts make it read as a template.

nodes.name: Editorial explainer collage
nodes.summary: Vox-style explainer graphics: collage, labelled diagrams, split-screen editorial panels and subtitles that move an argument forward one idea at a time.
nodes.detail:
Typical outputs are 15 to 60 s explainers where a process unfolds (a request moving through a system, a drink
built from labelled ingredients) or a numbered scene list is walked through.

**Execute:** give the explainer a start-to-finish process shape rather than a topic montage; budget about five
seconds per idea; name the audience and the narration method; require fact-checking; split the piece into
separately addressable scenes; cap words per frame. Naming a house style (Vox) hands the model a dense shared
vocabulary for layout, collage and pacing. Iterate in visible versions and compare them side by side.

**Why it works:** a structure fixed before visuals prevents generic montage and invented numbers, and one idea per
beat keeps comprehension ahead of motion.

**Failure modes:** text-heavy frames, rushed pacing that cuts narration early, little transition variety, missing
subtitles, hallucinated statistics (no explainer prompt in the gallery analysis asked for fact-checking).

nodes.name: Talking-head overlay b-roll
nodes.summary: Motion graphics layered over existing footage: full-frame cutaways, side-third transparent panels, HUD overlays, punch-in zooms and research b-roll keyed to the speaker's words.
nodes.detail:
Inputs are footage plus a timestamped transcript (SRT).

**Execute:** inspect the footage for resolution, fps and picture-in-picture layout; plan clips sentence by sentence
(full cutaway, side-third panel, or nothing); place panels in the third of the frame away from the face; render
panels with alpha (ProRes 4444) and cutaways as MP4; key animations to emphasis words. Density presets: medium
about three clips, heavy four to five, per roughly 30 s. Variants include head-tracking HUDs over AI video and
browser captures of real sources. Final assembly usually happens in the user's own editor.

**Why it works:** graphics that land on spoken emphasis feel edited rather than pasted on, and respecting the
existing composition keeps the speaker readable.

**Failure modes:** the skill cannot transcribe, so an SRT must be supplied; HUD perspective came out reversed;
first drafts are busy and need simplifying; default palette off-brand; around 15 minutes of generation per 30 s
of footage.

nodes.name: Paper-cutout stop-motion
nodes.summary: Tactile handmade look: gouache and crayon textures, torn-edge shapes with thin white outlines, a puppet-stage frame and stop-motion wobble at a reduced frame rate.
nodes.detail:
Seen in an educational Hawking-radiation explainer (curtain stage, child narrator) and in user-reported demos.

**Execute:** name the physical media explicitly (paper cutout, gouache, crayon, torn edges with a thin white
outline) and fix the palette; add small seeded jitter to outlines and hold each drawing for two frames (a 12 fps
feel inside a 24 or 30 fps master); demand medium-appropriate morph transitions (sun rays curling into a black
hole) instead of cuts; let a guide character carry the lesson. Generate narration per scene with an external TTS
and align scene timing to the clips.

**Why it works:** material language plus controlled imperfection removes the sterile vector look and signals craft.

**Failure modes:** the built-in synthetic voice sounded robotic and broke the storybook tone; unseeded jitter
flickers instead of wobbling; the chat sandbox cannot call external audio APIs, forcing a split workflow.

nodes.name: Low-res pixel art
nodes.summary: Pixel-art sequences rendered at a tiny internal resolution and animated at a deliberately low frame rate with hit-stop, or pixel-grid mascots composited into painted sets.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** render at a low internal resolution (e.g. 320x180) and upscale with nearest-neighbour; animate at
12 fps inside a 30 fps master so motion steps like genuine sprite work; freeze a few frames on impact (hit-stop);
treat pixel fonts carefully. clawd-video shows the hybrid variant: a pixel-grid mascot rebuilt from an exact
reference, with proportions written as numbers in comments, chevron pixel eyes for expressions, no ink outline,
dropped into a watercolor set.

**Why it works:** a period constraint hides model weaknesses and makes the style read as authentic rather than as
a smooth CSS tween; low frame rate is a style signal, not a defect.

**Failure modes:** pixel glyphs misread as other letters (caught only by snapshot self-review); smooth sub-pixel
motion that betrays the style; mirroring a sprite instead of drawing the flipped view.

nodes.name: Retro low-poly and voxel 3D
nodes.summary: Deliberately low-fidelity 3D (PS1-era low-poly scenes, seeded voxel worlds, voxel showreels) generated procedurally in Three.js.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** ask for a named period constraint (PS1 low-poly, voxel); generate terrain and props from seeded noise so
every render is identical; keep materials flat and lighting simple; drive slow orbit or dolly cameras from t. A
recurring showpiece is the continuous scale zoom (galaxy to atom).

**Why it works:** the constraint produces a coherent aesthetic at low effort and turns simple geometry into a
deliberate choice rather than a limitation; the model is strong at procedural code and weak at photoreal detail.

**Failure modes:** Three.js adds cost and complexity when the design is actually flat; unseeded noise breaks
reproducibility and makes stills checks meaningless; overlapping geometry; evidence for this register comes from
descriptions and summaries, not inspected renders.

nodes.name: 3D cinematic orbit
nodes.summary: Real 3D scenes (products, rooms, bouncing objects) with orbiting or pushing cameras, built in Three.js inside a timeline, or in Blender operated by Claude through MCP.
nodes.detail:
Two routes are evidenced. (1) A Three.js scene mixed into an HTML composition (HyperFrames with GSAP) adds depth
and camera motion to otherwise flat kinetic graphics; the camera is a pure function of t like everything else.
(2) Blender through the Blender MCP add-on: upscale 2D assets, convert them to 3D with a 2D-to-3D tool, let Claude
write Blender Python and operate the app, then render overnight.

**Why it works:** parallax, lighting and a moving camera lift perceived production value far above flat vectors.

**Failure modes:** overlapping buildings, unrealistic physics (rockets), weak explosions, low-quality 2D inputs
producing low-quality 3D models, long render times, and `will-change` on camera-scaled DOM elements blurring
text. Use it only when depth carries meaning; it is overhead for flat design.

nodes.name: Stick-figure doodle narrative
nodes.summary: Minimal line characters (stick figures, walking doodles with moving shadows) telling short stories drawn frame by frame in JavaScript.
nodes.detail:
Evidence is thin: a community post claims one-prompt stick-figure animation videos, a rumour roundup cites walking
doodles and a JS-drawn 30-second life story, and a compilation shows a hand-drawn JS short.

**Execute (inferred from adjacent sources):** draw each figure from a simple parametric rig whose joints are
functions of t; keep a contact shadow under the feet that shrinks with height; add seeded line jitter for a
hand-drawn feel; stage one readable action per beat with anticipation and settle.

**Why it can work:** minimal characters keep the model inside what it draws well and put the weight on timing and
staging, where the numbers-first animation table helps most.

**Failure modes:** flat, strictly-2D feel without narration and sound; one-prompt quality claims are unverified;
nothing in the corpus documents its pipeline.

nodes.name: Whiteboard vector diagram
nodes.summary: Hand-drawn-feel editable diagrams (Excalidraw, SVG) with a fixed shape grammar, used as the static base for diagram-building explainers.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** build native vector objects rather than raster images; reuse recurring objects (robot, cog, logo) and
save finished ones to a stencil library; give each shape a fixed meaning (for example square = changed item,
rounded = new component, double border = step); run a render-export-compare loop against the target image until
they match. For motion, these vectors become nodes revealed in sequence, and the shape key stays constant.

**Why it works:** a consistent visual grammar makes generated diagrams legible, and editable vectors remain
tweakable by hand after the agent finishes.

**Failure modes:** early iterations omitted text entirely, objects disappeared between iterations, labels landed in
the wrong place; a cheap model was fast but weak on detail while a strong one took about 16 minutes and ten times
the cost. The corpus shows static diagrams only, so animation of this register is extrapolated.

nodes.name: Interactive simulation explainer
nodes.summary: Explainers that open as a sketch and become a live, parameterised simulation (a 3D catapult, a rotatable airplane) the viewer can manipulate: generative UI rather than fixed video.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** open on a hand-drawn 2D sketch frame; on play, transition into a Three.js or canvas physics simulation
with sliders for the key variables (force, angle). A renderer decision matrix chooses the engine per request:
Three.js for 3D, canvas plus JS for simulations, D3 for graphs, Chart.js for charts, Tone.js for audio. Inject one
shared design-system stylesheet into every generated sandbox so all visuals share theme and spacing.

**Why it works:** the sketch-to-live reveal is a strong moment, and interaction turns explanation into
understanding.

**Failure modes:** about 15 minutes per generation; weaker models produce broken layouts, missing interactivity or
incomplete visuals; real-time interactive code is not directly renderable to MP4 unless it also exposes a
time-pure mode. Relevant to the atlas mainly as a sibling medium and a source of routing patterns.

nodes.name: Hybrid generative-plus-code cinematic
nodes.summary: Photoreal or cinematic shots from image and video generators combined with code-rendered typography, UI and diagrams in an editor.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** keep everything that must be exact (text, UI, data, logos) in code; generate photoreal people,
environments and asset sheets with external models (Higgsfield with Seedream or Seedance, Google Flow, a GPT image
model at 2K or above); have Claude write those generation prompts in the reference style; composite the results
in a timeline editor. In generator-only sequences, continuity comes from attaching the last frame of clip N as the
reference for clip N+1.

**Why it works:** each tool does what it is good at: code cannot produce photoreal people, generators cannot produce
crisp, exact text.

**Failure modes:** generator output is neither deterministic nor code-editable; free-tier credit limits (about three
10 s clips a day); style and composition drift between clips; the continuity handoff was shown on one example
only.

nodes.name: Kinetic typography
nodes.summary: Text as a moving design element: per-letter entrances, word morphs, in-world stickers and floaters, and lines that arrive on the beat.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** one typeface per piece; separate in and out timing for every text block so incoming and outgoing text
never overlap inside a morphing shape; per-letter animation when one word turns into another; a hard cap on words
per frame; entries aligned to beats or spoken emphasis. In cartoon work, in-world glyphs use a sticker treatment
(bold monospace, thick paper-coloured outline, bright fill) and a floater that pops in with easeOutBack overshoot
around 2.2, drifts up and fades.

**Why it raises quality:** at motion speed, legible type carries most of the meaning in launch films and explainers.

**Failure modes:** letter collisions during morphs; `will-change` on camera-scaled elements blurring text; fonts
missing in headless Chrome (bundle fonts or use common ones); corner text and centred-text-on-gradient defaults.

nodes.name: Morphing hero shape
nodes.summary: One object whose size, radius, fill and silhouette interpolate across states (circle, square, pill, card) and acts as the through-line of the piece.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** list the states as numeric targets (width, height, radius, fill, x, y); interpolate them with a shared
closed-form spring that has minimal overshoot; swap the inner content behind a short blur near the midpoint of the
morph; drive any attached element (chart bars, labels, connectors) from the same spring so it stays locked to the
shape. A cursor or a beat motivates each state change.

**Why it raises quality:** continuity of a single object is the clearest signal of intentional design and keeps
attention anchored across the whole clip; it also lets one rendering path handle many visual states.

**Failure modes:** content overlapping mid-morph when text lacks its own exit timing; overshoot large enough to look
cartoonish; morphing so fast it strobes without motion blur; the same morph repeated until it becomes a tic.

nodes.name: Camera move
nodes.summary: Virtual camera pushes, pans, orbits and impact kicks computed from t, often one continuous move across a whole piece.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** treat the camera as one transform applied to the whole stage in 2D, or a Three.js camera in 3D, driven
by easing curves of t. "One continuous camera move" is a feel-level direction that reads premium and works well
as designer feedback. On impacts, add a 0.3 to 0.5 s spring-damped camera kick, then hold still so the hit lands.
The per-frame speed limits apply to the camera as much as to objects.

**Why it raises quality:** controlled camera motion adds depth and guides attention without adding clutter.

**Failure modes:** generic camera shake (on the banned-effects list), `will-change` on scaled layers blurring text,
moves too fast for 24 fps, and camera motion that fights the subject's motion.

nodes.name: Connected transition
nodes.summary: Scene changes made by transforming something already on screen into the next subject, or by carrying a recurring element across, instead of a cut or crossfade.
nodes.detail:
Examples: sun rays curling into a black hole; a container reshaping into the next UI; a storyboard rule that every
lyric scene links into the next. In generator pipelines the equivalent is the last-frame handoff.

**Execute:** at each boundary, name the element that survives and what it becomes; compute the transition from the
outgoing scene's end state (values match at the boundary); vary the transition type across the piece; reserve hard
cuts for intentional punctuation. Crossfades sit on the banned-effects list for launch films; clawd-video allows a
0.4 s background crossfade only when a 30 s film is split into two painted scenes.

**Why it raises quality:** connected changes read as one designed piece rather than a slideshow of effects.

**Failure modes:** low transition variety, cuts that reset attention, mismatched values at the boundary causing a
pop.

nodes.name: Part-based character rig
nodes.summary: Characters assembled from ordered primitive parts with pivots, an origin at the feet, a body pose, per-part offsets and an eye or expression object.
nodes.detail:
**Execute (clawd-video pattern):** parts are ellipses, rects, rounded rects or polygons drawn in a fixed order; the
body pose is {x, y, sx, sy, rot, turn} with per-part rotation, offset and scale; the origin sits at the feet so
squash and stretch keep them planted; eyes have modes (normal, happy, closed) and scale for surprise; a spin uses
turn = cos(angle) and hides the face on the back view; hand world positions come from a point query so props can be
attached and the grip eased over about 0.15 s. Proportions are copied from a reference and written as numbers in
comments.

**Why it raises quality:** drawing from one rig every frame keeps the character on-model, and squash is just a
temporary scale of that rig.

**Failure modes:** limbs pivoting inside the body vanish when raised (pivot slightly outside); mirrored sprites read
wrong; parts poke out while "hidden".

nodes.name: Squash, stretch and anticipation curves
nodes.summary: Classic animation principles encoded as concrete curves: crouch before a jump, stretch on take-off, spring-damped squash on landing, volume preservation and follow-through lag.
nodes.detail:
**Numbers that work at 24 fps (clawd-video reference):** anticipation 0.15 to 0.3 s with sy 0.78 to 0.85 and sx 1.1
to 1.14; take-off stretch sy 1.25 to 1.3 easing to 1 over the first 35 percent of the hop; landing squash
sy = 1 - 0.3 * spring(t - tLand, 2.4, 7), settling in about 0.5 s; volume sx = 1/sqrt(sy) in the air; tilt plus or
minus 0.1 to 0.15 into the direction of travel on a parabolic arc; follow-through delay 0.05 to 0.1 s; small hop
0.3 to 0.4 s, big hop 0.55 to 0.8 s; blink 0.12 to 0.14 s; surprise eyes 1.45x.

**For motion graphics:** the same idea becomes entrance overshoot, stagger offsets and settle holds.

**Why it raises quality:** motion feels physical and characterful instead of linear.

**Failure modes:** bouncy easing applied everywhere (banned in launch films), exaggeration with no anticipation.

nodes.name: Particle layer
nodes.summary: Confetti, petals, snow, dust puffs and flying glyphs from seeded, analytic particle systems, drawn in two depth passes.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** compute each particle's position in closed form from t (an analytic drag-and-gravity solution rather
than step integration), so any frame can be rendered alone; give rain a sway term; let pieces come to rest on the
ground; fake a 3D flip with scale(1, cos). Precompute the event list (burst times, glyph spawns) from a seeded RNG.
Draw resting pieces before characters and flying pieces after them.

**Why it raises quality:** motivated bursts at a story payoff (success, celebration) add energy and texture while
staying deterministic.

**Failure modes:** generic particle bursts are one of the most-cited AI tells and sit on the launch-film banned
list; use them only where the story earns them. Integrated (stateful) particle sims break frame independence.

nodes.name: Grain and vignette finish
nodes.summary: A global finishing pass applied over every frame: low-frequency mottle plus fine noise in overlay blend, and a warm radial vignette in multiply.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** generate the grain and vignette textures once from a seeded generator; composite them over each
finished frame (overlay at roughly 0.26 to 0.28 alpha for day scenes, about 0.2 with a darker vignette such as
rgb(60,50,70) for night). Expose it as one config value so it can be disabled.

**Why it raises quality:** a single shared finish ties clean vector characters and painted backgrounds into one
medium, so the frame reads as made rather than assembled; it also softens the too-clean digital edge of code
output.

**Failure modes:** grain that changes randomly per frame becomes noise rather than paper; overdone vignette muddies
corners; on dark launch-film grounds a paper finish may clash with the requested look.

nodes.name: Painted texture layer
nodes.summary: Watercolor washes, blooms, pencil and ink strokes painted with p5.brush into cached background and prop canvases.
nodes.detail:
**Brush kit:** flat `wash` base; `water` for watercolor fill (big areas bleed 0.01 to 0.03, texture 0.5, border 0.1;
objects bleed 0.02 to 0.05, border 0.3 to 0.5); `blob` for soft blooms; `ink` with pen, HB, 2B, marker, charcoal
brushes; `shape` combining wash, shade and ink; `pigment` squares used as character fill patterns; `band` for
ground and sky.

**Recipe for a solid object:** wash a base, water a darker tone on top (opacity 90 to 120), add small light blobs,
ink the outline at weight 1.0 to 1.3. Build backgrounds back to front with a dark contact-shadow ellipse under each
object. Brushes are scaled 3.2 at 1080p.

**Failure modes:** pigment has no real transparency, so sprites are painted on paper and clipped 2 to 4 px outside
the ink (evenodd rings for holes); paint flipped views separately.

nodes.name: Cartoon FX vocabulary
nodes.summary: Small reusable effects (contact shadow, dust puffs, impact lines, surprise lines, camera kick, restrained glow, smear ghosts) that sell physicality.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** a contact shadow that shrinks and fades as the character rises (a large part of why jumps read); on an
impact, squash both objects, add impact lines and a puff burst, kick the camera for 0.3 to 0.5 s, then hold; for
surprise, freeze one or two frames, scale the eyes to 1.45x, add a small hop and lines over the head; glow uses the
`lighter` blend at alpha 0.1 to 0.2 with rays at 0.03 to 0.04; coloured light on characters uses `screen` tints;
one or two translucent past poses act as smear frames for fast moves.

**Why it raises quality:** a small, consistent vocabulary gives the model ready-made beats of emphasis without
inventing effects each time.

**Failure modes:** glow too strong washes the frame milky; source-over tints turn muddy; FX used without story
motivation become clutter.

nodes.name: Hit-stop and holds
nodes.summary: Freezing the action for a few frames at an impact, and holding still afterwards, so hits and reveals land.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** at the impact frame, stop all motion for two to four frames (pixel-art sections) or one to two frames
before a surprise take; after any impact or reveal, hold still for a beat before the next action; keep the last
0.5 s of a film calm because the video ends there. Holds are also where text gets read.

**Why it raises quality:** contrast between motion and stillness gives impacts weight and punch, and gives the viewer
time to register what changed. Without holds, everything is equally busy and nothing reads as important.

**Failure modes:** "long holds" appear on the launch-film banned list, so holds must be short and motivated rather
than dead air; a freeze without a matching sound hit can read as a dropped frame.

nodes.name: Data and diagram nodes
nodes.summary: Charts, bars, labelled nodes and flow arrows revealed step by step, driven by the same timing functions as the objects around them.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** drive chart values from the same spring that moves their container so bars and frame stay locked;
show relative bar sizes and skeleton text lines until real numbers are supplied; give diagram shapes fixed
meanings; reveal along the process order (input, step, output); choose the renderer per job (SVG for diagrams, D3
for graphs, Chart.js for charts, Three.js only when depth matters).

**Why it raises quality:** data that moves in lockstep with the layout reads as one designed system, and honest
placeholders keep polished graphics from shipping invented statistics.

**Failure modes:** hallucinated figures from one-line prompts; label collisions with characters or titles; empty
frames between reveals; weaker models producing broken diagram layouts.

nodes.name: UI moments and cursor driver
nodes.summary: Product screens reduced to three to five ordered UI moments, with a cursor that clicks, drags or types to motivate each transition.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** list the ordered UI moments in the brief's inputs block, with real screenshots or rebuilt UI in the
brand's colours and font; animate a cursor along eased arcs to the next target, with a press or click on the beat;
drive typing from an integrated phase table so a variable-rate rhythm stays deterministic (clawd-video accelerates
typing from 5 to 14 Hz by integrating the rate at 1/480 s steps and emitting a tap where the phase crosses an
integer); for loops, match cursor position and speed between the last and first frames.

**Why it raises quality:** the product stays the subject rather than a backdrop, and every change has a visible
cause.

**Failure modes:** generic placeholder UI, loop stutter, cursor teleporting between moments.

nodes.name: Captions and on-screen text track
nodes.summary: Subtitles and on-screen text derived from a timestamped transcript and timed to words.

nodes.name: Narration voiceover
nodes.summary: Narration generated by TTS one clip per scene, after which scene timings are aligned to the clip lengths.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** write the voiceover line for each scene in the storyboard; generate one audio clip per scene with an
external TTS (Fish Audio via API or MCP, ElevenLabs, edge-tts); measure each clip's duration and set scene lengths
from it, so picture follows audio rather than the reverse; mix under music with ducking.

**Why it raises quality:** narration turns flat animation into an explainer, and per-scene clips keep re-timing local
when a line changes.

**Failure modes:** default synthetic voices sounded robotic and broke the tone; the claude.ai chat sandbox cannot
call external APIs, so generation moves to Claude Code; an unnarrated structured build "felt flat"; mismatched
scene and clip lengths cause rushed or dead air.

nodes.name: Music bed on a beat grid
nodes.summary: Music synthesised in code or sourced from a service, with tempo derived from on-screen rhythm and an arrangement that follows the story.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** pick the tempo from the picture: BPM = 60 / period of the on-screen beat (a 0.4 s dance beat gives 150
BPM, grid offset to land on the hops), otherwise 110 to 130 BPM feels bouncy. Follow the story: sparse plucks for
an intro, bass and rising hat density while building, cut the music for 0.3 s on a problem, crash plus kick on the
exact success frame, a IV-V-I cadence into the settle. Launch films: kick per beat, riser into the final bar.
Rough gains: plucks 0.1 to 0.3, bass 0.25 to 0.35, kick 0.4 to 0.5.

**Why it raises quality:** music that shares the picture's grid makes cuts and hits feel inevitable.

**Failure modes:** off-taste tracks until corrected; uncertain benefit when retiming picture to an imposed track;
licensing for outside files.

nodes.name: Sound effect per action
nodes.summary: Every visible action gets a sound at an exported event time: boing for hops, thud for landings, whoosh for fast moves, a click per key tap, a chime on success.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** export event times from the same code that animates them; map action to sound with a lookup table
(hop, landing, impact, blink, peek or spin slide, whoosh, footstep, typing click, pop, glitch, chime with sparkle,
confetti popper); pan by screen x from -1 to +1; keep SFX above the music; make impacts the loudest moments and the
biggest story beat loudest of all. Rough gains: tiny SFX 0.05 to 0.1, landings 0.2 to 0.45, hero impact 0.8.
Calibrate taste on a short segment by auditioning 8 to 10 options.

**Why it raises quality:** sound sells weight and makes code animation feel finished.

**Failure modes:** SFX cannot be judged before a render; trial and error on taste; drift if times are typed by hand
instead of exported.

nodes.name: Guide character
nodes.summary: A narrator or mascot (a child narrator, a math-drawn robot guide) who carries the viewer through an explanation and across style changes.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** define the character once in a character bible (proportions, palette, expressions) and draw it from one
rig; let it point at, react to, or physically interact with the concept being explained; keep it consistent across
scenes even when the rendering style changes (pixel art, voxel, cartoon, kawaii, hand-drawn in one piece); give it
the narration lines.

**Why it raises quality:** a character turns an explanation into a story, which keeps viewers engaged and gives
abstract content a point of view to follow.

**Failure modes:** labels covering the character and jumps colliding with titles (caught by snapshot review); the
character drifting off-model when not drawn from a single rig; a guide used as decoration rather than as the
carrier of the lesson.

nodes.name: Verified research b-roll
nodes.summary: Screenshots, scrolling recordings and highlighted zooms of real sources, captured by the agent's browser and limited to verifiable facts.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** when the script cites a fact, product or brand, have the agent open the real source, capture a
screenshot or scrolling recording, and add a highlight and zoom on the key line; collect logos and product
screenshots for a named brand the same way rather than inventing them. Store captures in the project's reference
folder with their URL.

**Why it raises quality:** grounded b-roll is credible, and real brand material breaks the model's repetitive default
palette and house style.

**Failure modes:** browser tools need logins and connectors; unverifiable claims slipping in; capturing content the
project has no rights to use; screenshots that are too dense to read at motion speed.

nodes.name: Generated asset sheet
nodes.summary: Photoreal or illustrated assets generated externally in the reference style and dropped into a reference folder for code to animate.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** have Claude write an image-generation prompt for an asset sheet in the reference style; generate at 2K
or above with an image model (GPT image, OpenArt, Seedream); cut out the assets, logos and portraits; animate them
in code alongside vector type and UI. For 3D, upscale the 2D asset and convert it with a 2D-to-3D tool before
bringing it into Blender.

**Why it raises quality:** it offloads photorealism, which Claude renders poorly, while keeping motion, timing and
type under code control; a few crafted backgrounds raise perceived production value beyond pure vectors.

**Failure modes:** low-quality 2D inputs give low-quality 3D; style mismatch between generated assets and vector
elements; non-deterministic regeneration.

nodes.name: Logo sting and end card
nodes.summary: A 2 to 5 s logo intro or outro, or an end title (logo, URL, line), landing in the final half bar and followed by a calm settle.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** define the ending in the brief (logo, URL or line); land it in the final half bar of the beat grid; keep
the last half second calm; for logo stings, request several variants (for example five) in one batch and export
each as an MP4, then pick; check a still of the final frame for logo legibility (dark-on-dark invisible logos and
duplicated logos were real bugs).

**Why it raises quality:** the ending is what viewers remember and what loops back to the start; batches of variants
beat iterating on one draft.

**Failure modes:** abrupt endings with no settle, weak first or last frame, loop stutter when the end does not match
the start.

nodes.name: Seeded procedural field
nodes.summary: Terrain, props, textures or noise fields generated from fixed-seed noise, giving organic detail that is identical on every render.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** create every random value from a seeded generator (each paint job or system gets its own seed);
generate terrain, prop placement, layout jitter and grain from noise functions of position and, if animated, of t;
precompute expensive fields once and cache them. Ban `Math.random` outright.

**Why it raises quality:** rich, organic detail without nondeterminism, so stills checks, motion checks and
re-renders all see the same frame; changing the seed becomes a cheap way to explore variants.

**Failure modes:** unseeded randomness makes texture boil between frames and breaks reproducibility; per-frame
regeneration of an expensive field is slow; noise detail that is too fine aliases at video resolution.

nodes.name: 3D scene layer
nodes.summary: A Three.js scene embedded in a 2D composition and driven by the same timeline as the DOM and SVG layers.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** register the Three.js render as one more track on the seekable timeline, setting camera and object
transforms from t on every seek rather than from a requestAnimationFrame loop; keep geometry simple (bouncing
ball, product, low-poly world); composite it with GSAP-driven DOM and SVG type.

**Why it raises quality:** depth and camera motion lift otherwise flat kinetic graphics, and a shared timeline keeps
2D and 3D in sync.

**Failure modes:** extra cost when the design is flat; real-time loops that ignore the seek clock; text blurred by
transforms; GSAP or Three.js loaded from a blocked CDN failing the render (bundle locally).

nodes.name: Tweak panel
nodes.summary: An in-page control panel exposing colours, backgrounds, text sizes and layout variants so a human can tune taste directly.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** ask the output to include a small control panel (hidden in render mode) bound to the style tokens:
palette, background, type scale, layout variant, sometimes simulation parameters such as force and angle; when a
setting is chosen, write it back into the design system or the scene's parameters.

**Why it raises quality:** the human tunes taste parameters in seconds without another prompting round, and the
chosen values become explicit, reusable tokens rather than prose feedback.

**Failure modes:** the panel leaking into rendered frames; tuned values living only in the browser instead of being
saved; too many knobs inviting endless fiddling.

nodes.name: 1. Brief intake
nodes.summary: Settle every decision the model would otherwise guess: subject, single concept, duration, format, tempo, palette, type, avoid list, renderer and ending, using an inputs block, an interview or sensible defaults.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** collect a fixed inputs block (product name, one-line promise, three to five ordered UI moments, hex
colours, one font, light or dark, pixel format such as 9:16, length, tempo, avoid list, ending). Either interview
the user first (a project-level master prompt asking about theme, format, clip length, brand, pacing, audio) or
apply defaults instead of questions (1920x1080, 24 fps, 8 to 20 s, sound on); user-supplied timings are the
contract. Name the renderer explicitly. Optionally run a cheap "prompt bouncer" that rejects vague briefs.

**Why it matters:** long briefs that settle decisions beat the dominant 26-word one-liners, whose results ranged from
zero to around 17k likes with a median of 5.

**Output:** a brief file that every later stage reads.

nodes.name: 2. Reference teardown
nodes.summary: Gather proven reference videos, extract frames, and break them into palette, type, layout, motion, shot length, transitions and pacing, with explicit borrow and avoid lists.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** pick references (galleries that publish their prompts are ideal); download them and pull frames at
intervals; have Claude describe colour, typography, layout, camera moves, grain, text entry and exit, shot lengths
and transitions; merge across references into one summary with a list of moves to borrow and things to leave out
for this brand (e.g. white scenes). Copy the grammar, never the content, logos or characters. For known
characters, look up accurate reference art first.

**Why it matters:** the creator who measured it said the biggest gain came from showing references, not from a
cleverer prompt; references beat no references even though Claude never copies them exactly.

**Output:** a teardown note that feeds the style system.

nodes.name: 3. Style system and assets
nodes.summary: Distil brand and references into one persistent design-system file of look-and-motion rules, and gather or generate the assets the piece needs.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** write one file covering palette (hex), typeface, type scale, spacing, grain and finish, easing and
spring constants, transition grammar, banned effects with replacements, and house rules such as "every scene fills
the frame" and "nothing overlaps". Build it from the brand's site, logos and fonts, or from a reference site if
there is no brand; iterate on it for a few rounds and save a copy per client. Collect real brand screenshots and
logos; generate asset sheets externally for anything photoreal.

**Why it matters:** every video, deck and logo sting inherits the same tokens, so output stops drifting across scenes
and generations, and a rule fixed once stays fixed.

**Output:** design-system file plus an asset folder.

nodes.name: 4. Script and storyboard
nodes.summary: Write the script, scene list or clip plan (visual, on-screen text, voiceover line, transition per scene) and get it approved before any animation is built.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** produce a numbered scene list with, for each scene, the visual, on-screen text (within the word cap),
voiceover line and the transition into the next scene; for overlay work, a clip plan listing type (cutaway, panel,
none) and position. Make each scene a separately addressable unit so later comments target one scene. For long
pieces, write a STORYBOARD file plus an ANIMATION_GUIDE so parallel subagents can each build one chapter in the
same style.

**Why it matters:** it is the cheapest point to catch editorial and direction errors, and per-scene units keep
revisions local.

**Output:** an approved storyboard that the beat grid and stills derive from.

nodes.name: 5. Beat grid and timing map
nodes.summary: Fix the timeline numerically: a beat table in seconds or frames, tempo and bars, speech word timings or measured beats, with every change and cue placed on it.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** choose the timing master. Music-led: state BPM and bars, put a change on every beat, the hook in bar
one, the strongest moment in the last full bar and the end title in the final half bar; optionally synthesize the
track first and measure it into a beats file (beats, downbeats, hits) or detect beats in real audio with numpy.
Speech-led: derive word timings from the SRT and key graphics to emphasis words. Story-led: a beat table comment at
the top of the story file (about five beats for 15 s, one readable action per beat) plus blocking marks as named
constants. Review the grid as a table before coding.

**Why it matters:** beat-matched change separates launch films from slideshows and makes sound sync automatic.

**Output:** beat map, cue list.

nodes.name: 6. Key stills
nodes.summary: Render one poster-like still per scene type or per beat and review them before animating anything.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** with the frame-as-function-of-t architecture, a still is just a seek to a time; render one still per
scene type (Rogoff) or one per beat, and after each build step in a character piece (beat table, paint jobs, static
rig, pose function, FX). Review for clutter, overlaps, empty frames, readability and brand fit; fix layout bugs
here.

**Why it matters:** renders cost 11 to 20 minutes or more per cycle; stills cost seconds and caught real bugs such as
a duplicated logo and a dark-on-dark invisible logo.

**Output:** an approved stills set that becomes the visual contract for the build.

nodes.name: 7. Scene build
nodes.summary: Implement each scene as code against a fixed engine contract: a time-pure frame function plus motion tracks and an event-cue export.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** scaffold from a template whose engine stays fixed; Claude writes only the story or composition file.
The clawd-video contract is { finish, paint[], setup(), frame(t), track(t), cues() } with a config line for W, H, FPS,
DURATION. HyperFrames uses HTML clips with data-start, data-duration and track index plus a paused GSAP timeline
registered on window. Build in order, checking stills after each step: timeline, static layers, rig or layout,
motion, FX. Everything is a function of t with seeded randomness; prefer a declarative keyframe or track timeline
over long if/else beat branches (the clawd example ran to 1,391 lines). Build scenes as separate units, optionally
in parallel subagents.

**Why it matters:** a small, fixed writing surface keeps quality high and makes every frame inspectable.

nodes.name: 8. Render
nodes.summary: Capture frames deterministically in a headless browser (seek, screenshot, pipe) and encode them with ffmpeg, optionally blending subframes for motion blur.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** step exactly frame i at t = i / FPS; for motion blur capture three or four subframes per output frame
across a 180-degree shutter and blend them (ffmpeg `tmix`); encode H.264 (clawd-video uses preset slow, CRF 16,
tune animation) or ProRes 4444 for alpha panels; pass an exact frame count. Provide render modes: live loop,
freeze at `?t=`, fast stills, every-Nth samples, full render, audio-only rebuild. Surface script errors through a
global error hook. Use parallel, resumable workers for long pieces.

**Why it matters:** frame-exact capture cannot drop frames or drift from audio.

**Limits:** PNG-per-frame capture is fine for 15 s at 1080p (about 40 s on an M-series Mac) but will not scale to
minute-long 4K; consider WebCodecs or a framework renderer.

nodes.name: 9. Audio build
nodes.summary: Build the soundtrack from the exported cues: synthesized or sourced music on the beat grid, a sound effect per visible action, narration, then normalise loudness and mux.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** read the cue file written at render time; place music on a grid aligned to on-screen beats and an SFX
on every cue; add per-scene narration; mix with SFX above music and the biggest story beat loudest; normalise with
two-pass linear loudnorm to -16 LUFS, true peak about -1.5 dBTP; mux as AAC 192 kbps, 48 kHz. Keep an audio-only
rebuild path that takes seconds. The order can invert: some pipelines synthesize the track first and retime the
animation to measured beats.

**Why it matters:** sound locked to picture is what makes code animation feel finished; code synthesis also avoids
licensing risk.

**Caveat:** the model cannot listen, so this stage must be verified by meters and waveforms and reported honestly.

nodes.name: 10. QA and self-critique
nodes.summary: Look at the actual output: stills, samples, contact sheets, motion checks, spec probes and scored critique, then fix and repeat until gates pass.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** render key stills and every-Nth samples; build a frame-numbered contact sheet plus dense sheets around
fast actions; run the frame-jump detector; zoom into crops (sprite edges, faces in blinks, hands on props, depth
switches); probe the file spec; check loudness and the waveform; score against written criteria and repair the
lowest scores; optionally route stills to a panel of specialised critics (typographer, motion director, brand).
Treat v1 as a draft with a dedicated fix pass.

**Why it matters:** code can be correct and still look wrong; verifying is harder than generating, so the loop is
where most polish comes from. One cited film ran 163 calls over about seven hours.

**Output:** a pass/fail record per gate and an honest list of what could not be checked.

nodes.name: 11. Assembly and delivery
nodes.summary: Join segments, place overlays and audio on a timeline, run final technical checks, and hand over the MP4, the runnable project and an honest verification summary.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** for standalone films, the renderer's mux is the final step; for overlay and editing work, assemble in a
timeline editor (the user's NLE, Motion OS Editor, CapCut, Tella via MCP) or join with ffmpeg, stripping black
frames and checking sync. Provide review surfaces: a local viewer page, an original-versus-augmented comparison
page and a timing note. Deliver the video, the source project and a short statement of what was verified, what was
fixed and what could not be checked (the audio was not heard).

**Why it matters:** human timing tweaks on top of agent output avoid re-prompting the whole piece, and honest
delivery notes keep trust.

nodes.name: 12. Feedback to rules
nodes.summary: Turn every review round into durable rules: write fixes back into the design system and the skill's pitfalls list so the same mistake cannot recur, then confirm against a frozen benchmark.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** collect human notes as timestamped, point-anchored comments in problem-plus-fix-plus-keep form; apply
them one round at a time; at the end of each round tell the agent to learn from the session and update the skill
(one creator's style skill grew to about 1,400 lines and 36 rules); add any unrequested effect that showed up to
the banned list; add symptom, cause and fix rows to the QA table. For systematic tuning, change one instruction per
candidate, score it with a frozen, validated evaluator in isolated headless trials, keep or revert, then confirm on
held-out briefs.

**Why it matters:** compounding taste; this is the stage that makes the skill improve itself.

nodes.name: Custom seek(t) HTML page
nodes.summary: A single hand-written HTML file in which every visual is computed from a time value in one seek function, captured frame by frame by a headless browser.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** one page with a `seek(t)` (or `frame(t)`) entry point; DOM, SVG or Canvas drawn purely from t; no CSS
transitions, timers, `Math.random` or carried state; springs as closed-form step responses. Expose modes: live
loop, freeze at `?t=`, and render mode driven by the capture script. Variants: Slodyczka's motion.js engine, the
p5.js clawd engine, plain HTML plus Playwright in the prompt-motion gallery, and Ahmed's Canvas/SVG/Three.js pages.

**Why use it:** zero dependencies, the model already writes HTML well, and any frame is addressable for QA.

**Trade-offs:** Claude Code defaults to it unless a framework is named, so runs vary in stack unless the renderer is
specified; no editable timeline UI; capture speed limits length.

nodes.name: Remotion
nodes.summary: A React-based video framework that renders compositions frame by frame with its own renderer and timeline tooling.
nodes.detail:
**Use:** when you want scenes on an editable timeline, audio placement and a scalable renderer instead of
hand-rolled capture; compositions are already frame-indexed, which fits the time-pure rule. Mentioned as one of the
four rendering routes and as a harness option for 2D narrative animation.

**Trade-offs:** licensing may require a paid licence for some companies; it adds a build toolchain; the corpus gives
no inspected Remotion source, so specifics here are thin.

**Contrast:** HyperFrames keeps compositions as plain HTML with GSAP; Remotion uses React components.

nodes.name: HyperFrames
nodes.summary: HeyGen's open-source HTML-to-video framework: compositions are HTML clips with timing attributes plus a paused GSAP timeline, seeked frame by frame in headless Chrome and encoded with ffmpeg.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** each clip element carries data-start, data-duration and data-track-index; register a paused GSAP timeline
on `window.__timelines`; the renderer seeks each frame and encodes with ffmpeg; scenes appear on an editable
timeline and can mix DOM, SVG and a Three.js layer. Used for a 15 s showreel (about 90 minutes of agent time), 4K
editing-team animations and narrative shorts.

**Gotchas from its docs:** a GSAP script from a blocked CDN breaks the render, so bundle it locally; set start states
with `gsap.set` before building timelines; animate transforms and opacity, not layout properties; deterministic
rendering is Linux-only.

nodes.name: p5.js + p5.brush
nodes.summary: p5.js 2.x sketches with the p5.brush library for watercolor, pencil and ink painting, used to paint cached layers that are then composited per frame.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** run each paint job once on a hidden WEBGL p5 instance and copy it to a 2D canvas; draw moving parts per
frame on Canvas 2D; scale brushes by W/1920 (3.2 at 1080p). Used in clawd-video and in PDoomVideo, a music video
whose storyboard and animation guide briefed parallel subagents.

**Gotchas:** needs p5 2.x and WEBGL, origin at the centre (the engine translates); the page needs a UTF-8 charset
meta or p5 fails with a regex error; pigment mixes with what is beneath, so there is no true transparency; long
polygon edges bleed in sawtooth unless subdivided; repainting per frame is slow and flickers. p5.js is LGPL-2.1,
p5.brush MIT.

nodes.name: GSAP
nodes.summary: A JavaScript tweening and timeline library used inside HyperFrames compositions as a paused, seekable timeline.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** build all tweens on a paused timeline and let the renderer seek it, never letting it play on wall-clock
time; set initial states with `gsap.set` before adding tweens; animate transforms and opacity rather than layout
properties; bundle the library locally because a blocked CDN silently breaks headless renders.

**Why use it:** a mature, expressive easing and sequencing vocabulary the model knows well, which makes staggered
kinetic type and UI choreography quick to write.

**Failure modes:** using it in play mode (non-deterministic), layout-property animation causing reflow jitter, bouncy
default eases that read as template.

nodes.name: Three.js
nodes.summary: WebGL 3D library used for product orbits, low-poly and voxel worlds, mixed 2D/3D compositions and interactive simulations.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** set camera and object transforms from t on each seek; generate geometry procedurally from seeded noise;
keep materials simple; for interactive explainers, expose parameters through sliders; route 3D requests to it via a
renderer decision matrix rather than using it by default.

**Why use it:** depth, parallax and camera motion that 2D cannot fake.

**Failure modes:** added cost for flat design; real-time render loops ignoring the seek clock; overlapping geometry
and unconvincing physics; GPU differences between machines (headless Linux falls back to slow SwiftShader in some
setups).

nodes.name: Puppeteer / Playwright capture
nodes.summary: Headless Chromium driven by Puppeteer or Playwright to seek each frame, screenshot it and pipe it to an encoder.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** load the page in render mode, wait for a ready flag, then for each frame call the page's seek or frame
function and capture (clawd-video exports a PNG with toDataURL and pipes it to ffmpeg image2pipe); capture several
subframes for motion blur; run parallel, resumable workers for long pieces; surface page errors through a global
error variable.

**Why use it:** frame-exact capture decoupled from real-time performance, so slow frames never drop.

**Failure modes:** missing fonts in headless Chrome; Puppeteer downloading its own Chrome on first run; slow
SwiftShader on Linux; PNG-per-frame capture too slow for minute-long 4K; pageerror timeouts from a single JS error.

nodes.name: ffmpeg
nodes.summary: The encoder and swiss-army tool of the pipeline: encode, blend subframes, mux audio, normalise loudness, build contact sheets and probe the result.
nodes.detail:
**Roles evidenced:** image2pipe ingest; H.264 encode (preset slow, CRF 16, tune animation), ProRes 4444 for alpha
panels; `tmix` to blend subframes into motion blur; two-pass linear `loudnorm` to -16 LUFS; `ebur128` loudness
measurement; `showwavespic` waveform image; `select` plus `tile` contact sheets with frame numbers; `crop` for zoomed
detail checks; joining segments, stripping black frames and checking A/V sync; `ffprobe` for size, fps, frame
count, duration and streams.

**Why it matters:** most machine gates are one ffmpeg command, which makes them cheap enough to run every iteration.

nodes.name: Code-synthesized audio
nodes.summary: Music and sound effects written as code (a Node synth, the Web Audio API, Python) and rendered to WAV, so audio is original, length-matched and placed at exact cue times.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** clawd-video's Node synth offers Karplus-Strong plucks, FM bells, drums, chords and about 20 cartoon SFX,
placed from the cue file and mixed to WAV; launch-film builds use Web Audio for a kick per beat, a riser into the
last bar and hits on scene changes; other creators had Opus compose music in Python or write a small JS synth for
whooshes and hits; procedural SFX such as square waves for jumps and filtered noise for paper.

**Why use it:** zero licensing risk, exact sync and a seconds-long rebuild.

**Limits:** the model cannot hear the result; taste needs human calibration; one creator found the benefit of
retiming to synthesized beats uncertain.

nodes.name: AI voice and music services
nodes.summary: External TTS and music providers (Fish Audio, ElevenLabs TTS and Music, edge-tts, Suno, Epidemic Sound via MCP) used for narration and licensed or generated music.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** call them from Claude Code (the chat sandbox cannot reach external APIs); generate narration one clip per
scene and time scenes to the clips; pick music from a licensed library via MCP or generate songs for music videos;
mix with ffmpeg under synthesized SFX.

**Why use them:** voice quality far above built-in synthetic voices, and fuller music than code synthesis.

**Failure modes:** licences and logins required; robotic default voices; cost; tone mismatch; less exact sync than
code audio unless re-timed from measured durations.

nodes.name: Whisper / Parakeet transcription
nodes.summary: Local speech-to-text (whisper.cpp, NVIDIA Parakeet) or a speech API that produces a timestamped SRT, the sync backbone for speech-led work.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** install a local model (allow the model-download domains in the sandbox's network settings) or call an
API; output SRT; estimate word timings from segments; use it to cut awkward pauses, place captions and key
graphics to words.

**Why use it:** without timestamps there is nothing to sync graphics to; local models avoid upload of client
footage.

**Failure modes:** the b-roll skill itself cannot transcribe and requires an SRT; misspelled names in auto
transcripts; segment-level timing is coarser than word level.

nodes.name: Generative image and video models
nodes.summary: Image and video generators (Higgsfield with Seedream and Seedance, Google Flow, GPT image, OpenArt) used for photoreal shots and asset sheets that code cannot render.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** Claude writes the generation prompts in the reference style; generate assets at 2K or above, or 10 s clips
per scene; continuity via last-frame references; composite with code-rendered type and UI in an editor.

**Why use them:** photoreal people, environments and cinematic shots are outside what code renders well.

**Failure modes:** non-deterministic and not code-editable; credit limits; style drift; the code-only constraint
("built in code, no image or video model") is sometimes the better choice for brand-exact, editable output.

nodes.name: Blender via MCP
nodes.summary: Blender driven by Claude through the Blender MCP add-on, with Claude writing Blender Python for 3D cinematics.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** connect the MCP add-on; upscale 2D assets and convert them to 3D; let Claude build scenes, cameras and
lights through Blender Python and operate the app (computer use where needed); render overnight.

**Why use it:** real 3D lighting and materials beyond Three.js scenes.

**Failure modes:** overlapping buildings, unrealistic physics and weak explosions in the demo; low-quality inputs make
low-quality models; long renders; a single-source, demo-level pipeline with no QA gates described.

**Atlas stance:** treat as an experimental route; any adoption should add the same stills and probe gates used for browser renders, since no deterministic seek or QA path is documented.

nodes.name: Timeline editors
nodes.summary: Human-facing editors (the user's NLE, Motion OS Editor, CapCut, Tella via MCP) used for final assembly and timing tweaks on agent-rendered output.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** export panels with alpha and cutaways as separate files, then place them in the editor; or let the agent
drive an editor through MCP (Tella cuts); make final timing adjustments by hand without re-prompting.

**Why use them:** human timing judgment on top of agent output is cheaper than another full render cycle.

**Failure modes:** edits made in the editor are not written back to the project or the rules, so they are lost to
the next run; logins and connectors required; agent-built editor clones were laggy with weak transitions.

nodes.name: Claude design system and live artifacts
nodes.summary: Claude's built-in design-system feature and live HTML artifacts with canvas comments, used to build brand-aligned explainers scene by scene and export MP4.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** create and iterate a design system from brand assets and save it; attach it to every request; build
each storyboard scene as a separate unit inside a live artifact; comment on specific scenes; export to MP4; turn
repeatable formats into skills and scheduled tasks.

**Why use it:** tight loop between design tokens, preview and comments without a local toolchain.

**Failure modes:** chat sandbox cannot call external APIs (audio must be done in Claude Code); whole-video iteration
without scene separation confuses the model; copy often needs rewriting.

nodes.name: Excalidraw CLI skill
nodes.summary: An Obsidian Excalidraw command-line tool plus agent skill that lets coding agents build native, editable Excalidraw drawings and export PNGs for comparison.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** enable the CLI (plugin 2.29 or later); give the agent a sandbox vault with copied reference images; point
it at the skill repository; it builds the drawing, exports a PNG, compares with the target and iterates; save
finished objects to a stencil library.

**Why use it:** editable vector output plus a built-in vision loop.

**Limits:** static diagrams only in the evidence; costs rose about tenfold with the stronger model.

**Transfer to motion:** the export-compare loop is the reusable part; for animated diagrams, export stills at beat times and compare each with the storyboard frame rather than a single target image.

nodes.name: Frame is a pure function of t
nodes.summary: Every frame is computed only from its timestamp: no carried state, no CSS transitions, no timers, no wall-clock animation.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** expose one `frame(t)` or `seek(t)`; inside a beat compute progress with a segment helper
seg(t, t0, t1) shaped by an easing; when a later beat depends on an earlier one, recompute it (a shared carry(t)
for the prop and the character); write springs as closed-form step responses; compute particles analytically.

**Why it is the top lever:** it is the precondition for everything else: rendering any frame in isolation, stills
review at any time, frame-exact capture regardless of capture speed, motion-jump detection between neighbouring
frames, exact frame counts, audio cues that cannot drift, and reproducible A/B comparison of skill versions.

**Failure if broken:** dropped or duplicated frames, flicker, renders that differ run to run, QA that checks a frame
the final video never shows.

nodes.name: Seeded randomness only
nodes.summary: All randomness comes from seeded generators, one seed per system or paint job, with `Math.random` banned.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** a small seeded RNG in the engine core; every paint job, particle system, layout jitter and noise field
gets its own seed; precompute event lists (glyph spawns, bursts) from seeds at setup; change seeds deliberately to
explore variants.

**Why it raises quality:** organic variation without nondeterminism, so texture does not boil, re-renders match, and
seed becomes a controllable creative parameter.

**Failure if broken:** jitter that flickers rather than wobbles, painted texture that changes every frame, renders
that cannot be reproduced for a fix, false positives in frame-diff checks.

nodes.name: Motion blur by subframe blending
nodes.summary: Fast motion is smeared rather than strobed: blend three or four subframes per output frame across a 180-degree shutter, or draw one or two translucent ghost poses.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** in the capture loop, seek to several sub-times inside each frame's shutter interval (e.g. four subframes
over half the frame duration) and average them, or render at 60 fps with three subframes and blend with ffmpeg
`tmix`; blur then scales automatically with speed. For cheap cartoon smears, draw past poses at 1/48 s and 2/48 s
behind, skipping hidden poses.

**Why it raises quality:** removes the strobing, too-clean look that marks code animation, especially on fast
morphs, and lets motion exceed the speed limits without breaking up.

**Costs and failures:** render time multiplies by the subframe count; blur on text makes it unreadable during
moves, so pace text to settle before reading.

nodes.name: Per-frame speed limits
nodes.summary: Motion above about 60 px per frame or 0.7 rad per frame at 24 fps, or cycles above about 5 Hz, reads as strobing and must be slowed, spread or smeared.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** compute a track(t) of key channels (x, y, scale, angle) for every moving subject; compare neighbouring
frames against per-channel limits (clawd-video: 60 px, 0.25 scale, 0.7 rad per frame); keep walk and run cycles at
or below 5 Hz (4.8 or more frames per cycle); fast repeating actions such as typing may exceed it because they read
as a blur, but keep big limbs slower. Limits scale with fps; recompute for 30 or 60 fps.

**Why it raises quality:** turns a perceptual judgment into a number the model can check without watching the video.

**Failure if ignored:** stutter on hops and runs, camera moves that break up, morphs that pop.

nodes.name: Banned-effects list with replacements
nodes.summary: One line of five to nine banned default effects, each paired with an alternative, that grows by adding whatever unrequested effect appeared in the last run.
nodes.detail:
**Typical bans:** glows, particle bursts, lens flares, crossfades, bouncy easing, corner text, generic gradients,
camera shake, RGB split, long holds, centred text, "anything template-like". Pair each with a replacement (a
crossfade becomes a connected morph; bouncy easing becomes a near-critically damped spring; a gradient becomes a
flat ground with one accent).

**Why it raises quality:** blocks the model's default AI-looking moves, which are the most-cited tell; a ban without
a replacement leaves a hole the model fills with another default.

**Execute:** keep it in the rules file, not the per-run prompt; after each run, add any effect nobody asked for.

**Failure modes:** an ever-longer list that bans what a style needs (cartoon glow is fine under caps), so lists are
per style.

nodes.name: One-object continuity
nodes.summary: Name one concept and keep one subject alive: every shot grows from the previous one through a morph or a recurring element, never a reset.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** state the single concept in the brief; pick the hero object or motif; design each transition as a
transformation of what is on screen; reuse one dot, line or container as a motif across the piece; keep one rig per
character drawn every frame.

**Why it raises quality:** observed across several independent sources as the difference between designed motion and
a slideshow of effects; it also reduces cognitive load because the viewer tracks one thing.

**Failure modes:** the morph becomes a repeated tic with no variety; continuity forced where a deliberate cut would
punctuate better; text inside the continuous object colliding during changes.

nodes.name: Beat-locked changes
nodes.summary: Visual changes land on a stated grid: musical beats, spoken emphasis words, or the story's beat table.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** fix tempo and bars in the brief (e.g. 120 BPM, change every beat, hook in bar one, peak in last full bar,
end title in last half bar); for speech, key changes to word timings from the SRT; for character pieces, a beat
table with one readable action per beat, merging beats rather than rushing them. Derive music tempo from on-screen
periodic motion when the picture leads.

**Why it raises quality:** the clearest measured difference between launch films and feature slideshows; edits that
land on rhythm feel intentional.

**Failure modes:** changes on every beat with no hierarchy (monotone), rhythm imposed on a story that needs holds,
speech cut early to fit the grid.

nodes.name: Cue-locked sound
nodes.summary: Sound effects and musical hits are placed from event times exported by the animation code itself, so picture and sound share one source of truth.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** the story exposes `cues()` returning event times (hops, taps, impacts); the renderer writes them to a
cue file; the score reads the file and places SFX and hits; variable-rate rhythms are integrated into a phase table
so taps are discrete, deterministic events shared by visuals and audio; rebuild audio alone in seconds.

**Why it raises quality:** nothing can drift, every visible action gets a sound, and the hit lands on the exact
frame.

**Failure modes:** hand-typed times drifting after a timing edit; sounds for actions that were removed; audio built
before final timing without a re-sync.

nodes.name: Two-pass loudness normalisation
nodes.summary: Normalise the mix with two-pass linear loudnorm to about -16 LUFS integrated with a true-peak ceiling, keeping impacts punchy.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** measure in pass one, apply linear gain in pass two (ffmpeg `loudnorm` linear mode) to -16 LUFS with true
peak around -1.5 dBTP; verify with `ebur128` that integrated loudness is about -16 and peak at or below -1 dBFS;
export AAC 192 kbps, 48 kHz.

**Why it raises quality:** consistent platform loudness without the dynamic compression that single-pass or dynamic
mode applies, which flattens impacts.

**Failure if ignored:** clipped audio, flattened hits, inconsistent loudness between pieces in a series.

nodes.name: Paint once, composite per frame
nodes.summary: Expensive, textured or generative layers are rendered a single time and cached; only moving parts are drawn per frame.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** run paint jobs (backgrounds, props, pigment swatches, noise fields, blurred backgrounds) once at setup
into cached canvases; draw everything that moves as clean vectors on top; anything that moves in the background
must be drawn per frame rather than baked; occlusion redraws the cached background clipped to the occluder's
outline.

**Why it raises quality:** rich organic texture with zero flicker and low render cost; the pattern generalises to any
expensive generative layer.

**Failure if ignored:** watercolor that boils between frames, slow renders, inconsistent texture across stills.

nodes.name: Animation principles as numbers
nodes.summary: Taste is written as parameters: anticipation durations, stretch and squash ratios, spring constants, follow-through delays, hold lengths and per-frame limits, in a reference table the model applies.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** keep a numbers-first table in the skill (anticipation 0.15 to 0.3 s, take-off sy 1.25 to 1.3, landing
spring freq 2.4 damp 7, volume sx = 1/sqrt(sy), follow-through 0.05 to 0.1 s, blink 0.12 to 0.14 s); for motion
graphics, extend it with entrance overshoot, stagger offsets, hold durations and exit timing; add story-shape
templates (8 s: intro 2, action 3, payoff 2, button 1; 15 s: intro 3, task 4, problem 3, success 3, bow 2).

**Why it is a top lever for an LLM:** it converts "make it bouncy" into repeatable, checkable values and is the
biggest single reason the clawd output looks crafted.

**Failure modes:** numbers applied without staging judgement; constants tuned for 24 fps used at 60.

nodes.name: Typographic and palette restraint
nodes.summary: One typeface, at most three colours plus black and white, a warm off-white or near-black ground with one accent, and a word cap per frame.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** set these in the design system and the brief; cap words per slide or frame; give text separate in and out
timings; keep the character or hero element the most saturated, highest-contrast item; derive colours from the
brand rather than the model's default black-and-orange.

**Why it raises quality:** restraint reads as premium and keeps frames legible at motion speed; overloaded frames are
one of the most common review notes.

**Failure modes:** the default palette returning when unconstrained; dark-on-dark logos; brand colours that fail
contrast at small sizes.

nodes.name: Numeric caps on light and texture
nodes.summary: Effects that are allowed carry hard ceilings: glow alpha at or below 0.15 to 0.2, rays at or below 0.04, grain about 0.26, coloured light only through screen or lighter blends.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** encode the caps in the style reference; use `screen` for coloured light on characters and `lighter` for
glows, never source-over; apply lighting only as a tint on top that never changes a base colour; keep a soft-light
overlay at or below 0.15.

**Why it raises quality:** highlights without washing out the frame or muddying colour; a refinement of the banned
list for styles where some glow belongs.

**Failure if ignored:** milky, washed-out frames during glow; green over orange turning to mud.

nodes.name: Constrained springs and shared drivers
nodes.summary: Use closed-form springs with very small overshoot plus exponential easing, and drive linked elements from the same spring so they stay locked.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** springs as analytic damped responses of t (no integration state); overshoot small for motion graphics
(lively but not cartoonish), larger only for deliberate cartoon squash; exponential ease-outs for entrances; one
spring function moves a container and its chart, label or connector together.

**Why it raises quality:** motion feels alive and physical without the bouncy-easing tell, and synchronized elements
never slip apart.

**Failure modes:** independent eases on linked parts drifting; overshoot that reads as template bounce; springs
integrated per frame, which breaks time purity.

nodes.name: Continuity at beat boundaries
nodes.summary: Where two timeline segments meet, values must match or blend, so nothing pops; snaps are reserved for impacts.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** start each beat from the values the previous one ended on, or blend from the previous end pose into the
new one over about 0.14 s with a recursive numeric lerp of nested pose objects; mark intentional snaps (take-off,
impact, flung arm) so the jump detector can whitelist them.

**Why it raises quality:** one-frame pops at beat changes are a classic sign of piecewise animation code.

**Failure if ignored:** characters or containers jumping a few pixels at every boundary, which the viewer feels as
jitter even without spotting it.

nodes.name: Staging: one action at a time
nodes.summary: Stage one readable action at a time, look before acting, hold after impacts, switch depth only when clear, and end calm.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** in each beat, one primary action in silhouette; the character looks at its target before acting;
hold still after an impact so it lands; change depth (behind to in front) only when fully clear of the occluder,
usually at the top of a hop; keep the last 0.5 s calm; merge beats rather than rush them; put key moments on the
timeline first, then anticipation before and settle after each.

**Why it raises quality:** readability: the viewer always knows where to look. The same law applies to motion
graphics as one focal change per beat.

**Failure modes:** busy frames where several things move at once (an early-draft note from multiple creators).

nodes.name: One global finish
nodes.summary: A single finish layer (grain, vignette, shared colour treatment) is applied to every frame so mixed elements read as one medium.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** define the finish once in the story config or design system and composite it last; keep it identical
across scenes; when mixing code with generated assets or footage, apply the same grade and grain to both.

**Why it raises quality:** ties vector characters, painted sets, generated assets and UI into one coherent image; the
lack of a shared finish is why hybrid pieces often look pasted together.

**Failure modes:** per-scene finishes that drift; finish values that differ between preview and render; a grain
that changes randomly per frame.

nodes.name: Brand grounding
nodes.summary: Real brand inputs (palette, fonts, logos, screenshots, a saved design system) are fixed constraints for every piece, overriding the model's default house style.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** build the design system from the brand's site and assets before any motion; attach it to every request;
have the agent gather real screenshots and logos itself when only a brand name is given; inject one shared
stylesheet into every generated sandbox; give brand colours as hard inputs.

**Why it raises quality:** without it the model drifts to a repetitive default palette (black and orange) and generic
layouts; with it, every video, deck and sting matches.

**Failure modes:** design systems need several iteration rounds; references carrying off-brand moves unless an avoid
list exists; using a mascot or trademark you do not own in client work.

nodes.name: Data honesty
nodes.summary: Never invent figures or facts: use relative bars and skeleton text until real numbers arrive, require fact-checking for explainers, and show only verifiable sources.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** a hard rule in the skill that charts show relative size only and text uses placeholder lines when data is
missing; explainer briefs name the fact source and require checking; research b-roll captures the real page; flag
any number in the storyboard that lacks a source.

**Why it raises quality:** polished graphics make hallucinated stats more convincing and more damaging; credibility is
part of production value for explainers and client work.

**Failure modes:** short prompts producing fake statistics; placeholders accidentally shipping; none of the gallery's
explainer prompts asked for fact-checking.

nodes.name: Composition awareness
nodes.summary: Graphics respect the frame: every scene fills it, nothing overlaps, panels avoid the speaker's face, and text stays clear of characters and titles.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** inspect footage for layout before planning; place panels in the free third of the frame; write house
rules such as "every scene fills the frame" and "nothing overlaps" into the design system; check bounding boxes of
text, characters and logos for collisions in stills; keep safe margins for platform UI on vertical formats.

**Why it raises quality:** collision and covering bugs were among the most frequent defects found by self-review
(a label covering the character, a jump hitting the title).

**Failure modes:** empty frames, overlapping labels, panels covering the subject, reversed perspective on overlays.

nodes.name: Style-specific frame rate and imperfection
nodes.summary: Run handmade styles at deliberately low frame rates (12 fps holds inside a 30 fps master) and add seeded line jitter, so each style reads as genuine.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** quantise t to the style's frame rate for pixel-art and stop-motion sections while the master stays at
24 or 30 fps; jitter line paths with a seed that changes per held drawing, not per output frame; reserve smooth 60
fps with motion blur for UI and kinetic type.

**Why it raises quality:** removes the sterile vector look and avoids handmade styles moving like CSS tweens.

**Failure modes:** jitter that changes every output frame (flicker), low frame rate applied to UI where it reads as
lag.

nodes.name: Seamless loop closure
nodes.summary: For looping social clips, the last frame matches the first in position, speed and content, so the loop has no stutter.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** design the ending to return to the opening state; match cursor position and velocity, dot positions and
type between the last and first frame; verify by rendering frames 0 and N-1 side by side or diffing them; strengthen
