the opening frame because it doubles as the thumbnail and the loop point.

**Why it raises quality:** a visible stutter on loop is an instant amateur tell on platforms that autoplay.

**Failure modes:** a weak opening frame (noted in the morphing b-roll demo), an end card that cannot loop, velocity
mismatch even when positions match.

nodes.name: Fixed render contract
nodes.summary: Name the renderer and lock the spec (size, fps, duration, frame count, codecs) up front, so runs are reproducible and comparable.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** one config line sets W, H, FPS, DURATION and slug; total frames = FPS x DURATION and the encoder is told
that count; audio is cut to the duration; the brief names the renderer (plain HTML plus Playwright, Remotion,
HyperFrames, Three.js) instead of letting the agent choose; a render-contract section opens the project rules file.

**Why it raises quality:** an unnamed renderer means a different stack each run, which defeats comparison and rule
accumulation; exact specs make probe gates possible.

**Failure modes:** off-by-one durations, a different stack per run, fps changes that silently invalidate speed limits.

nodes.name: Render-safe web code
nodes.summary: Write web animation that survives headless capture: transforms and opacity only, explicit start states, local libraries and fonts, no will-change on scaled text.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** animate transform and opacity, not layout properties; set start states (`gsap.set`) before building
timelines; bundle GSAP, Three.js and fonts locally instead of loading from CDNs; include a UTF-8 charset meta; avoid
`will-change` on camera-scaled elements; load engine scripts before the story file; expose a global error variable.

**Why it raises quality:** most render failures are environmental, not creative; these rules remove whole classes of
silent breakage.

**Failure modes:** blank or timed-out renders, blurred text, misspelled glyphs from missing fonts.

nodes.name: Plan and storyboard approval
nodes.summary: A cheap checkpoint on the clip plan, script or storyboard (stills plus motion notes) before any build or render.
nodes.detail:
**Check:** each clip or scene has its on-screen text, type and position or visual, VO line and transition; density
matches the preset; one concept is named; word caps are respected; nothing requires invented data.

**Who:** a human in client work; for autonomous runs, a critic subagent or a rubric can stand in, with the human
gate kept for high-stakes pieces.

**Why:** it catches editorial and direction errors at the lowest cost, and is the step most creators credited with
avoiding wasted renders.

nodes.name: Key-stills review
nodes.summary: Render one still per scene type or per beat and inspect each at full size before animating or rendering the full piece.
nodes.detail:
**Check:** clutter, overlaps, empty frames, readability, brand fit, logo visibility; zoom into crops of edges, faces,
hands on props. Machine-assisted: bounding-box collision checks, contrast of text against its local background,
text pixel size at output resolution.

**Why:** seconds per still versus 11 to 20 minutes or more per render; caught duplicated and invisible logos and
layout bugs in practice.

**Pass rule:** every scene type has an approved still; no unresolved collision.

**Metrics to log:** number of stills reviewed, defects found per still, collisions detected, minimum text contrast ratio, minimum rendered text height in pixels.

nodes.name: Frame-numbered contact sheet
nodes.summary: Tile sampled frames from the rendered video with frame-number labels, plus dense sheets around fast actions, and read them.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** ffmpeg `select` plus `tile` (e.g. every 12th frame in a 4-wide grid for the overview; every 2nd frame
across a specified range for a fast action); label each tile with its frame number; open the image and look.

**Check:** continuous motion through fast actions, no missing or duplicated poses, consistent finish, correct depth
at switches.

**Why:** gives a model that cannot watch video a way to see motion over time in one image, and frame numbers make
fixes precise.

nodes.name: Frame-jump detector
nodes.summary: Compare a numeric track of each subject between neighbouring frames and list every jump above per-channel limits, so only intentional snaps remain.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** the story exposes track(t) with channels such as x, y, sy and rot; the tool samples it at every frame and
reports frames where the delta exceeds limits (clawd-video: 60 px for x and y, 0.25 for scale, 0.7 rad for angle);
the author whitelists intentional snaps (take-offs, impacts).

**Pass rule:** zero unexpected jumps.

**Why:** catches beat-boundary pops and strobing without anyone watching the video; possible only because frames are
a pure function of t. Extend it for motion graphics with per-element tracks (container size, text position, camera).

nodes.name: Vision self-review of snapshots
nodes.summary: The model captures stills of its own render, inspects them against the brief or a reference image, and fixes defects it was not told about.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** render, export PNGs, view them, compare with the target or style guide, list defects, fix, repeat.
Real catches: a label covering the character, a jump colliding with the title, a pixel glyph misreading as another
letter, missing text, misplaced labels, objects that vanished between iterations.

**Why:** verifying is harder than generating; the model cannot see problems in source code that are obvious in
pixels.

**Weakness:** self-review is agreeable; pair it with machine checks and specialised critics.

**Make it less agreeable:** give the reviewer a defect checklist (collision, cut-off text, misread glyph, missing element, off-brand colour) and require it to name at least one candidate defect per still before declaring a pass.

nodes.name: ffprobe spec check
nodes.summary: Probe the final file and assert size, fps, exact frame count, duration and stream presence; also strip black frames and check sync.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** `ffprobe -count_frames` to read codec, width, height, frame rate, number of frames read and duration;
assert frames = FPS x DURATION and that an audio stream exists; for assembled edits, detect black frames and check
A/V sync with ffmpeg before human review.

**Pass rule:** exact match to the render contract.

**Why:** a one-line, fully automatic gate that catches the off-by-one and missing-stream errors humans miss.

**Metrics to log:** width, height, r_frame_rate, nb_read_frames, duration, codec, audio stream present, black-frame count. Any mismatch is a hard fail with no human judgement needed, which makes this the cheapest gate to automate in an RSI loop.

nodes.name: Loudness and waveform check
nodes.summary: Measure integrated loudness and true peak with ebur128 and render a waveform image to confirm hits land where the story's impacts are.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** ffmpeg `ebur128=peak=true` for integrated LUFS and peak; `showwavespic` for a waveform PNG at video width;
overlay or compare spike positions with the cue file times.

**Pass rule:** about -16 LUFS, peak at or below -1 dBFS, spikes at impact cues, intentional quiet stretches only, no
clipping.

**Why:** the model cannot hear, so this is the only machine evidence about the mix; the delivery note must still say
the audio was not listened to.

**Extend:** compute the time offset between each cue in the cue file and the nearest waveform peak; report the maximum offset in milliseconds as a sync metric.

nodes.name: Scored critique threshold
nodes.summary: The model scores its render against written criteria, fixes the lowest scores and repeats until every criterion clears a threshold (about 7 to 8 out of 10) or a budget runs out.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** list criteria in the brief (continuity, beat sync, legibility, brand fit, restraint, ending); score each
out of 10 with a justification; fix the lowest; re-render the affected part; stop at threshold or budget. A variant
instructs the model to iterate until output matches the reference style.

**Why:** replaces part of the human review loop and makes progress visible.

**Weakness:** self-scores inflate; one cited example ran 163 calls over about seven hours; validate the rubric
against human judgment.

**Calibration:** keep a small set of human-rated renders and check that the self-scores rank them in the same order before trusting the threshold; log score deltas between iterations to detect inflation.

nodes.name: Specialist critic panel
nodes.summary: A chair session routes stills or storyboards to several persona critics (typographer, motion director, brand lead) who score, cross-examine and vote.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** round one, each critic scores out of 10; round two, critics respond to each other with some assigned to
argue against their own preference; round three, vote and chair verdict with conditions. Weight critics by
relevance and invoke only the top subset per question to keep cost down.

**Why:** distinct lenses give sharper review than one generic self-critique and counter agreeable scoring.

**Weakness:** evidenced only in a business-decision tool, not yet on motion output; agent teams cost more without
always answering better.

nodes.name: Timestamped human review
nodes.summary: Human notes pinned to a timestamp and an x/y point on the frame (or a sketch drawn over a frame), returned to the model as a batch.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** review the cut in a viewer that lets you pin comments to time and position; write each note as problem
plus fix plus what to keep; batch them; for spatial intent, draw directly on a still (the reversed-HUD fix); apply a
fix pattern across similar clips.

**Why:** unambiguous, local edits instead of vague whole-video feedback; the model gets 80 to 90 percent there and
human direction covers the rest.

**Feeds:** the feedback-to-rules stage.

**Metric:** count of notes per minute of video, and the share of notes that repeat a previously recorded rule (a repeat means the rules file failed).

nodes.name: Frozen, validated evaluator
nodes.summary: The grader used to tune a skill is built and proven first (broken input fails, reviewed good output passes, tampering is rejected), then frozen, with held-out confirmation.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** assemble a fixed evaluator from machine checks; prove it on known-bad and known-good renders; treat
timeouts as failures; run trials headless in bare mode with fixed model, effort, tools, turns and time; compare the
winning skill against the original on held-out briefs, alternating run order; cap budget and attempts in advance.

**Why:** a skill tuned against an untested checker learns to game it; a validated checker makes improvements real.

**Evidence note:** demonstrated on Python bug fixing, not motion; the transfer is direct but unproven here.

nodes.name: Fixed-prompt regression benchmark
nodes.summary: A standing set of reference briefs (a one-shot showreel, a fixed scene) rerun on every model or skill version and compared side by side.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** keep a fixed showcase prompt and a few fixed scenes; rerun them after each skill change or model upgrade;
place successive versions side by side (and an original-versus-augmented comparison page for overlay work); log
gate metrics per version.

**Why:** makes improvement measurable and catches regressions; also supplies portfolio material.

**Weakness:** likes and gut feel are noisy quality proxies (same prompt ranged from 0 to about 17k likes), so pair
the visual comparison with the machine metrics.

**Practice:** freeze the benchmark briefs, seeds, model, effort and renderer; store each version's outputs and metric table so any new version is compared on identical inputs.

nodes.name: Vague-prompt bouncer
nodes.summary: A cheap model check rejects briefs that do not settle the key decisions and suggests the missing fields before the main agent runs.
nodes.detail:
**Execute:** a small model or classifier inspects the brief for the inputs-block fields (duration, format, tempo,
palette, type, avoid list, renderer, ending, single concept); missing fields bounce back with suggestions or
defaults.

**Why:** directly addresses the one-liner problem that produces generic motion; it is cheaper to fix a brief than a
render.

**Evidence note:** shown as a generic Claude Code mod, not on motion briefs.

**Metric:** fraction of inputs-block fields filled before build; a brief below a set fraction (for example 80 percent) is returned with the missing fields listed and proposed defaults attached.

nodes.name: Generic AI look
nodes.summary: Template output: centred text, generic gradients, glows, lens flares, particle bursts, bouncy easing and the model's default black-and-orange palette.
nodes.detail:
**Cause:** no references, no brand context, no banned list; the model fills every unsettled decision with its
defaults.

**Symptoms:** scenes that look like a feature slideshow, interchangeable across brands; the same colour scheme
across unrelated briefs.

**Fix:** reference teardown, a design system from the brand, a banned-effects line with replacements, one concept
with connected transitions, beat-locked timing.

**Detect:** scan the composition source for banned primitives (gradient fills, glow filters, lens-flare or shake code, centred text over full-bleed gradients), compare used colours against the design-system palette, and have a critic flag frames that could belong to any brand. Every hit becomes a new line in the banned list.

nodes.name: One-liner variance
nodes.summary: Short, open briefs produce wildly inconsistent results run to run; even maximum effort does not remove the variance.
nodes.detail:
**Evidence:** one 26-word prompt in the gallery produced results from zero to about 17k likes with a median of 5;
several creators found structure, references and pacing plans were what turned inconsistent one-shots into reliable
output.

**Fix:** a decision-settling brief over 100 words or an inputs block, named renderer, beat grid, avoid list and review
step; keep one-liners only as discovery or benchmark prompts.

**Detect:** word count and inputs-block coverage of the brief before the run; variance across repeated runs of the same brief on the benchmark set. High variance means the brief, not the model, is underspecified.

nodes.name: Strobing fast motion
nodes.summary: Fast moves break into discrete jumps instead of reading as motion, because per-frame displacement exceeds what the eye fuses at the frame rate.
nodes.detail:
**Thresholds (24 fps):** about 60 px or 0.7 rad per frame, cycles above about 5 Hz.

**Symptoms:** stutter on hops, runs, morphs and camera moves; the too-clean look of unblurred code animation.

**Fix:** slow down or lengthen the move, spread it across more frames, add subframe motion blur or ghost smears;
verify with the frame-jump detector and dense contact sheets.

**Detect:** per-channel deltas from track(t) against the limits, scaled to the actual fps; optical-flow or pixel-difference spikes between neighbouring frames of the rendered MP4 as a fallback for elements without a track.

nodes.name: Beat-boundary pop
nodes.summary: A one-frame jump where two timeline segments meet because the end values of one do not match the start of the next.
nodes.detail:
**Cause:** piecewise animation code (one branch per beat) with independently written targets.

**Symptoms:** small twitches at every beat change, visible in dense contact sheets and flagged by the jump detector.

**Fix:** start each segment from the previous end values, or blend poses over about 0.14 s; whitelist only intended
snaps. A declarative track timeline that interpolates between keyframes avoids the class entirely.

**Detect:** evaluate the pose or layout at t0 minus epsilon and t0 plus epsilon for every beat boundary in the beat table and report any channel difference above a small tolerance that is not on the snap whitelist.

nodes.name: Nondeterministic frames and flicker
nodes.summary: Frames that differ between runs or boil between neighbours: Math.random, CSS transitions, timers, real-time loops, or brush textures regenerated per frame.
nodes.detail:
**Causes:** randomness without seeds, wall-clock animation, state carried between frames, repainting textured layers
each frame, an unnamed renderer that changes stack each run.

**Symptoms:** flicker or texture boiling, renders that cannot be reproduced for a fix, stills that do not match the
final video, broken loops.

**Fix:** time-pure frames, seeded RNG, paint-once caching, a fixed render contract.

**Detect:** render the same frame twice (and the same short range in two separate runs) and diff the pixels; any nonzero difference fails. Grep the source for Math.random, setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame and CSS transition declarations.

nodes.name: Text overload and busy frames
nodes.summary: Too much text and too many simultaneous moves per frame, unreadable at motion speed.
nodes.detail:
**Evidence:** "ask for less text" and "too busy, needed simplifying" were recurring notes; social frames overload
unless word limits are set.

**Fix:** word caps per frame, one action or focal change per beat, holds long enough to read, separate text in and out
timing, fewer clips at a lower density preset.

**Detect:** count words per scene from the storyboard and per sampled frame from the composition's text nodes; measure how long each text block is fully visible and compare with a reading-time budget (words divided by a reading rate).

nodes.name: Overlap and collision bugs
nodes.summary: Labels covering characters, jumps hitting titles, letters colliding inside morphing containers, text placed wrongly, objects vanishing between iterations.
nodes.detail:
**Cause:** the model reasons about layout in code and cannot see the pixels; text inside changing shapes lacks its
own timing.

**Fix:** key-stills review and vision self-review; bounding-box collision checks per sampled frame; house rule that
nothing overlaps; separate enter and exit timing for text.

**Detect:** at every sampled frame, collect bounding boxes of text, characters, logos and panels from the DOM or from the story's track output and report intersections that are not declared as intentional; also check boxes against the frame edge and the safe area.

nodes.name: Hallucinated data
nodes.summary: Invented statistics, figures and facts rendered convincingly inside polished graphics.
nodes.detail:
**Cause:** short prompts leave content gaps that the model fills with plausible numbers; explainer prompts rarely ask
for fact-checking.

**Fix:** data-honesty rule (relative bars and skeleton text until real data arrives), fact source named in the brief,
verified research b-roll, a storyboard check that flags unsourced numbers.

**Detect:** extract every number and named claim from the storyboard and on-screen text, and require each to map to a supplied source or an explicit placeholder; unmatched numbers fail the plan gate. Re-run the same check on the final composition, since numbers can enter during the build as well as in planning.

nodes.name: Wasted renders and wrong direction
nodes.summary: Spending long render cycles (minutes to hours) on a direction that review then rejects, or polishing a fundamentally weak concept.
nodes.detail:
**Evidence:** renders of 11 to 20 minutes, about 15 minutes per 30 s of b-roll, 90-minute showreel runs, and a
seven-hour, 163-call film.

**Fix:** plan approval and key-stills gates before rendering; preview stops for palette and design notes; when the
output is neither premium nor on-brief, change the subject or references (fix the right layer) rather than polish.

**Detect:** log render minutes spent before the first approved still and before the first approved storyboard; a high ratio of renders to approvals signals that gates are being skipped.

nodes.name: Reference copying
nodes.summary: Copying a reference's content, logos or characters instead of its grammar, or carrying over moves that do not suit the brand.
nodes.detail:
**Fix:** an explicit instruction to copy grammar never content; borrow and leave-out lists in the teardown; original
designs preferred; no trademarked mascots in client deliverables (clawd-video itself is an unaffiliated fan project
with no licence file, so study its patterns rather than copying code).

**Detect:** compare stills against reference frames for near-duplicate composition, identical text or logos; a perceptual-hash similarity above a threshold triggers review. Keep references in a separate folder so their assets cannot be imported by accident. Record which references informed each scene so provenance is auditable.

nodes.name: Feedback amnesia
nodes.summary: Review notes applied once but never written into the skill or design system, so the same errors return next run.
nodes.detail:
**Fix:** end every round with a "learn from this session and update the skill" step; write each fix into the design
system; append unrequested effects to the banned list; add symptom, cause and fix rows to the QA table; also write
back hand edits made in timeline editors.

**Detect:** tag each review note with a category and check it against the rules file; a note matching an existing rule means the rule is not being applied, while a note matching nothing means a rule is missing. Track the repeat-note rate across runs as the main health metric of the self-improving loop.

nodes.name: Headless environment failures
nodes.summary: Renders that time out or come out wrong for environmental reasons: missing charset meta, script order, CDN-blocked libraries, missing fonts, page errors.
nodes.detail:
**Examples:** p5 fails without a UTF-8 charset; engine scripts must load before the story; GSAP from a blocked CDN
breaks HyperFrames; missing fonts turn glyphs odd; a pageerror means a JS error in the story file; first run is slow
while Chrome downloads; Linux may fall back to slow SwiftShader.

**Fix:** render-safe code rules, local bundles and fonts, a global error hook, a template proven to render before any
edits.

**Detect:** a smoke render of the untouched template before editing; a font check that lists fonts actually used by the page; a timeout with the page's error variable printed.

nodes.name: Audio blindness
nodes.summary: The model cannot hear its mix, sound effects cannot be judged before a render, and single-pass normalisation silently flattens impacts.
nodes.detail:
**Fix:** cue-locked placement so timing is right by construction; loudness and waveform checks; two-pass linear
loudnorm; calibrate SFX taste with a human on short segments; say plainly in the delivery note that the audio was not
listened to.

**Detect:** integrated loudness and true peak via ebur128; peak-to-cue offsets from the waveform; silence detection on stretches that should carry sound; clipping count. None of these says whether the mix sounds good, so taste calibration on short segments with a human remains necessary, and the delivery note must say the audio was not heard.

nodes.name: Rushed or flat pacing
nodes.summary: First drafts that cut speech early, cram beats, lack transitions and variety, or feel flat and strictly 2D without narration and sound.
nodes.detail:
**Evidence:** first drafts that felt rushed, were too simple and had little transition variety; a structured but
unnarrated build felt flat; the model cannot reliably invent pacing alone.

**Fix:** supply a pacing plan and beat grid; merge beats rather than rush them (about five beats per 15 s, five
seconds per idea); add holds, narration and sound; vary transitions.

**Detect:** compare each scene's duration against its narration length and word count; flag scenes with less than the budgeted seconds per idea, beats shorter than the minimum action time, and transitions of the same type in a row.

nodes.name: Evaluator gaming and overfitting
nodes.summary: A skill tuned against a grader that can be fooled, or against a handful of demo briefs, improves its score but not its output.
nodes.detail:
**Examples:** a grader that can be edited, timeouts counted wrongly, extending attempts until a version looks lucky,
overfitting to three dev briefs, likes used as the quality signal.

**Fix:** frozen, validated evaluator; one change per candidate; held-out confirmation; fixed attempt counts and
budgets set in advance.

**Detect:** run the evaluator on known-bad and known-good renders every round; any drift in those control results means the evaluator or its environment changed. Keep held-out briefs that the optimiser never sees and require wins there too.

nodes.name: Weak opening and loop stutter
nodes.summary: A weak first frame, an abrupt or busy ending, or a loop whose last frame does not match its first.
nodes.detail:
**Evidence:** the morphing b-roll demo's opening frame was weak; mismatched first and last frames stutter on loop.

**Fix:** treat frame 0 as a designed poster (it is also the thumbnail); land the end title in the final half bar and
keep the last 0.5 s calm; for loops, match position, speed and content between the last and first frame and check
both stills side by side.

**Detect:** render frame 0 and the final frame as stills for every review; for loops, compute pixel and track differences between them; score the opening frame as a standalone poster in the critique rubric.

nodes.name: Director's brief
nodes.summary: A long structured brief that casts the model as director, animator, sound designer and render engineer and fixes style, character, transitions, a timestamped scene list and notes.
nodes.detail:
**Structure (merged from sources):** logline; references; tools and APIs; STYLE block (named media, palette); CHARACTER
bible; TRANSITION rules (e.g. no hard cuts, medium-appropriate morphs); SCENES with timestamp, visual, voiceover
line and transition; on-screen text; NOTES on tone, music, SFX and specs; workflow gates; critique loop;
deliverables. Roughly twelve parts in the fullest version.

**Why it works:** one-shot coherence; creators reported quality rising noticeably as prompt structure increased.

**Risk:** long briefs that mix decisions and wishes; keep hard rules in the rules file and creative intent in the
brief.

nodes.name: Inputs-block template
nodes.summary: A reusable template that exposes every likely-to-change decision as a field, or interviews the user for them, before the build proceeds without further questions.
nodes.detail:
**Fields:** product or subject, one-line promise, single concept, three to five ordered UI or story moments, hex
colours, one font, light or dark, pixel format, length, tempo and bars, avoid list, renderer, ending, audience and
narration method for explainers.

**Variants:** a master prompt stored in project instructions that runs a setup Q&A and then emits numbered per-clip
prompts with avoid lists; a published reference prompt reused with brand inputs swapped in; "ask for inputs first,
then a beat map and stills, then build without further questions".

nodes.name: Reference-teardown prompt
nodes.summary: Ask the model to analyse references for colour, typography, layout, motion and pacing and return a borrow list and a leave-out list, copying grammar never content.
nodes.detail:
**Pattern:** "Analyse these references: colours, typography, layout, motion, pacing, shot lengths, transitions, camera,
grain, text entry and exit. Merge into one summary. List the moves to borrow and the things to leave out for this
brand. Copy the grammar, never the content, logos or characters." Then: "write a shot list in that style."

**Why it works:** turns taste into an explicit, reviewable vocabulary and blocks off-brand carry-over.

**Output contract:** a structured note with sections for palette (hex values sampled from frames), type, layout grid, average shot length, transition inventory, camera moves, finish, borrow list and leave-out list. The sections map directly to fields in the design-system file.

nodes.name: Rules file that grows
nodes.summary: A project-level rules file (render contract, look and banned list, sound, feedback loop, things-that-bite) that the agent rewrites after every review round.
nodes.detail:
**Structure:** render contract; look section with bans and replacements; sound guidance; feedback-loop stage; a
things-that-bite list of hard-won pitfalls; a symptom, cause and fix table; a pre-delivery checklist. Keep one
instructions file (agents.md) rather than syncing several.

**Growth rule:** after each round, "learn from this session and update the skill"; one creator's grew to about 1,400
lines and 36 rules. Changes should be single, attributable edits so their effect can be measured.

**Discipline:** each new rule carries the date, the symptom that triggered it and the gate that will catch it next time; rules that never fire again can be retired, which keeps the file from bloating.

nodes.name: Word caps per frame
nodes.summary: State a maximum word count for each frame, slide or scene, and ask for less text by default.
nodes.detail:
**Pattern:** include an explicit cap in the brief or design system (the corpus gives the pattern, not a number; a
working default is a few words per kinetic beat and one short sentence per explainer scene); combine with "one idea
per scene" and around five seconds per idea.

**Why it works:** prevents the model from overloading frames, which keeps them readable at motion speed.

**Make it checkable:** express the cap as a field in the design system (words per frame, words per scene) so a script can count words in the storyboard and composition and fail the plan gate when a scene exceeds it. Pair with a minimum on-screen time per word so text that fits the cap still stays long enough to read.

nodes.name: Designer-style feedback
nodes.summary: Feedback written as problem plus fix plus what to keep, anchored to a timestamp and screen point, including feel-level direction, one round at a time.
nodes.detail:
**Pattern:** "At 0:04, top-left: the logo disappears on the dark ground. Put it on the accent panel. Keep the push-in."
Feel-level notes ("one continuous camera move") are allowed; batch the notes; revise one round at a time; when a
rough sketch communicates spatial intent better, draw on the frame. Event-keyed instructions ("zoom when I say zoom")
work for speech-led edits.

**Why it works:** precise, actionable revisions that preserve what already works, and that can be written straight
into rules.

**Write-back:** each note that reflects a general preference is converted into a rule in the rules file or a token change in the design system, with the note's timestamp as provenance.

nodes.name: Open showreel benchmark prompt
nodes.summary: A short, high-ambition brief ("make a 15 s showreel of yourself as a motion designer, go all out") used for discovery and as a fixed cross-model benchmark.
nodes.detail:
**Use:** discovery of what the model will choose when unconstrained, a standing benchmark rerun on every model or
skill version, and portfolio material. Frame it with a duration and shot count (15 s, six to eight shots).

**Limit:** high variance and long runtimes (about 90 minutes for 15 s); never the production path. Same prompt A/B
tested across models showed differences in shapes, assets and animation.

**Benchmark hygiene:** fix the seed, renderer and effort; store every output with its metrics; never tune the skill on this prompt alone, or the benchmark stops measuring generality.

nodes.name: Defaults instead of questions
nodes.summary: Ship sensible defaults (size, fps, length, sound on) so the agent can start immediately; treat user-given timings as the contract.

nodes.name: Progressive-disclosure skill layout
nodes.summary: A short main skill file that points to reference files loaded only at the matching step, with trigger-rich frontmatter and optional classifier routing.
nodes.detail:
**Pattern:** SKILL.md holds the workflow and the things-that-bite list; references (style, characters, animation,
sound, QA) load at their step; frontmatter lists many trigger phrases plus "even if they don't name the skill"; a
renderer decision matrix routes to the right engine; a classifier router can load only the top few skills.

**Why it works:** deep domain rules available when needed, context kept lean otherwise.

**For a motion skill:** split references by stage (brief, style, timing, animation numbers, audio, QA) so each stage loads only its file, and keep the banned list and render contract in the always-loaded core.

nodes.name: Single-change skill edit
nodes.summary: Each candidate revision of the skill changes exactly one instruction, so its effect on scores can be attributed and reverted.
nodes.detail:
**Pattern:** an optimiser prompt that may edit only the skill file, against a fixed metric; one change per candidate,
visible in the diff and traceable in transcripts; keep or revert; success framed as a checkable number, not "make it
better".

**Why it works:** attributes gains to specific rules (for example one banned-effects line) instead of bundled guesses;
the core move of an RSI loop.

**Bookkeeping:** record each candidate's diff, metric table and keep or revert decision in a log, so the history of the skill is a list of measured, attributable changes.
